diseases.name: Common Smut
diseases.description: A fungal disease that turns parts of the ear, tassel or stalk into swollen galls full of black spores.
diseases.causes: Spores survive in the soil for years and infect young, growing tissue, mostly through wounds from hail, insects or cultivation.
symptoms: Silvery-white, swollen galls on the ear, tassel or stalk
Galls darken and burst, releasing black powdery spores
Kernels replaced by galls on infected ears
diseases.effect: Infected ears are lost; the rest of the plant is usually fine.
diseases.untreated: Spores from burst galls add to the soil supply for years.

steps.title: Cut out galls before they burst
steps.instruction: Remove galls while they are still white and firm, bag them and take them away.

steps.title: Avoid wounding plants
steps.instruction: Take care when weeding and control ear-feeding insects.

steps.title: Balance the fertiliser
steps.instruction: Avoid heavy nitrogen and manure on the field.
steps.rationale: Lush, soft growth is more easily infected.

prevention.title: Grow tolerant hybrids
prevention.detail: Sweet corn varieties differ a lot in how often they get smut.

prevention.title: Remove galls every season
prevention.detail: Spores last for years in the soil.

prevention.title: Rotate fields
prevention.detail: Fewer spores where maize was not grown recently.

lifecycle: Spores survive in the soil and on debris.
They blow or splash onto young ears, tassels and stalks.
Infected tissue swells into silvery galls.
Galls burst and release black spores.
conditions: Wounds from hail, insects or tools.
Hot, dry weather followed by rain.
